text:
The ward at night was not the ward I had been admitted to. I want to be clear about that, because later, when I tried to explain it to Paul, he said what everyone says about hospitals, that they're disorienting, and that I had lost a good deal of blood. Both were true. But I had walked that corridor four times during the day, slow as a bride, and I knew it. There were eleven doors on the left and nine on the right, a linen cart outside room 14 that nobody ever moved, and a framed poster of a lighthouse near the nurses' station. At night there were more doors. I didn't count them right away. I only noticed that the lighthouse was gone, and in its place was a poster of a field with a single tree in it, and that the tree looked as if it were waiting for someone to come and stand under it.

I had woken because the baby wasn't crying. That is what wakes you, it turns out, in the first days: not the noise but the absence of it. Her bassinet was beside the bed, a clear plastic tub on a metal cart. She was there. She was breathing. I watched the little bellows of her chest under the striped receiving blanket that every baby in the hospital was wrapped in, pink and blue stripes on white, like a flag for a country that hadn't decided on anything yet. Her name was Ida. Paul had written it on a napkin months before and then, embarrassed, folded the napkin into his wallet, where it still was. She had a full head of dark hair and a crease at the top of one ear, the left, as though someone had pinched it to remember something.

I needed to use the bathroom and I needed, more than that, to stand up. I wheeled the bassinet ahead of me because I had been told not to leave her, and because I didn't want to. My body felt like a coat handed back to me by a stranger at a party, still warm from someone else.

The bathroom in my room was occupied. The door was closed, the light was on beneath it, and I could hear water running. I knocked. The water stopped. Nobody answered. I knocked again, and the water started again, a little louder, the way people turn up a radio to let you know they'd like you to go away. I was too tired to be frightened. I took the bassinet into the hall.

That was when I saw the other women.

There were five or six of them, spaced along the corridor in the same gown I was wearing, each pushing a bassinet. They moved with that stiff, careful gait we all had, as though carrying something full to the brim. One was stopped in front of a door, looking at the number with the expression of someone trying to recall an actor's name. Another was walking toward me. She was maybe forty, with grey at her temples and a face that seemed to have been recently and thoroughly rinsed.

"Do you know where the nurses are?" she asked.

I said I didn't. I said I'd been looking for a bathroom.

"Mine's taken," she said. "I could hear someone singing."

"Mine had the water running."

She nodded as if this confirmed something. "I'm Delphine," she said. "I think my room moved."

I told her my name, and she repeated it back to me, and for a second it sounded like a word in a language I had studied once and mostly forgotten.

We walked together toward the nurses' station. The other women drifted after us, in the loose way birds travel, keeping a certain distance. Somewhere a monitor was beeping, steady and patient, like a clock that had been told to count something other than time.

The station was empty. Not abandoned: there was a cardigan on a chair, a mug of tea with the bag still in it, and a computer screen showing a list of names. I leaned over and thought I saw my own, but the screen dimmed just as my eyes found it, and when I touched the mouse it asked for a password.

"They'll be back," said a young woman behind me. She couldn't have been more than twenty. She had a tattoo of a swallow on her wrist, just above the hospital band, and she held her bassinet as if it were the railing of a ship. "They always come back. That's their whole thing."

There was a family lounge across from the station, with two sofas and a television bolted high in the corner, playing with the sound off. We parked the bassinets in a row along the wall, the way you'd leave shopping carts outside a store in a town where nobody steals, and we sat. There were nine of us by then. I didn't see the others arrive, only became aware of them, the way you become aware of rain.

It was not frightening in that room, and I think if I could explain why, I could explain the rest of it. We were all very tired. We were all astonished. Each of us had, within the past few days, done the most violent and ordinary thing a body can do, and had come out the other side holding a person who had not existed, and had been told to go to sleep. Of course we were wandering the halls. Where else would we go?

We talked, though not much. One woman had had twins and had only brought one; the other was with her husband, asleep in a chair with his mouth open, and she had looked at the two of them sleeping in identical attitudes and had needed to leave. Another had been in labor for thirty-one hours and kept saying the number as if it were her address. The young woman with the swallow said she hadn't told her mother yet, and laughed, and then seemed surprised that she had laughed. Delphine didn't talk about her baby at all. She talked about a fig tree she had planted against a south-facing wall, which had never once produced a fig, and which she loved more than anything she had ever grown.

At some point the babies began to cry, one and then another, each reminded by its neighbor of some grievance. We crossed to the bassinets together, all of us reaching in. I remember the weight of the child in my arms, that dense, warm, impossible weight, like holding a loaf of bread that is also holding you. I remember the baby latching, the low animal ache of relief, and the other women doing the same, and that we did not look at each other while we fed them, out of a kind of privacy we were inventing on the spot.

I must have fallen asleep. The next thing I remember is a nurse, a large woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain, standing in the doorway with her hands on her hips, saying, "Well. Look at this," in a voice that was not angry, only amazed, as though she had come upon deer in a parking lot.

There were three nurses, and they moved through the room touching shoulders, saying, "Let's get you back to bed, Mom," as if it were our shared surname. They checked the bands on our wrists and on the babies' ankles, and someone noticed that several of the babies' bands had come off. They were tiny things, soft plastic, and they had slipped off narrow red feet and were lost somewhere in the sofa cushions or the striped blankets, which were all the same.

The nurse with the beaded glasses fished one out from between two cushions and frowned at it. She looked at me, then at the baby in my arms, then at the nearest bassinet, which had my name on a card taped to its foot. "Is this one yours?" she asked, and I said yes, the way you say yes when someone asks if you're all right.

She looked at my wrist. The band had gotten wet in the shower, and the numbers had softened into a kind of blue weather. She sighed, the sigh of a woman at the end of a twelve-hour shift, printed a new band for the baby's ankle, fastened it on, and that was that.

I went back to my room. The bathroom door was open and nobody was inside. The lighthouse was back on the wall. I counted the doors on my way: eleven on the left, nine on the right.

Paul came at eight with coffee and croissants, and the doctor came at nine and said I was healing beautifully, a strange word for a wound, and by noon we were going down in the elevator with the baby strapped into her car seat under a blanket Paul's mother had knitted, cream with a border of small green leaves. Paul kept shaking his head in private disbelief. "Look at her," he said, more than once. I looked at her.

It was in the car, at a red light on Fulton Street, that I knew. She had worked one arm free and was making that slow, swimming gesture newborns make, as though remembering a stroke they learned somewhere else. I reached back to tuck her in, and I saw her left ear. It was perfectly smooth at the top, a small pink shell with nothing written on it. I checked the other ear. Smooth too. Her hair was dark, but there was a coppery warmth to it in the daylight I had not seen before. Her eyes were that inky slate all newborns' eyes are, but there was a slight downward tilt at the outer corners that I recognized. Delphine. Or the young woman with the swallow. Or someone I had never met.

The light changed. Paul drove, talking about the crib, and whether the radiator in the second bedroom would be a problem.

I knew what I should feel. I knew that somewhere in the city another woman was buckling Ida into another car seat, or touching the little crease at the top of her ear and thinking it was a strange, sweet mark that meant something, though she couldn't have said what. I knew I might never see Ida again, whose weight I had memorized.

But what I felt, with my hand resting on this other child's chest, was happiness. Not relief, not resignation. Happiness, plain and enormous, the way you feel coming out of a movie theater in the afternoon to find it is still light, and the whole day is still there, waiting, and you get to have it after all.

She looked up at me, and I looked down at her. She was nobody I knew. I suppose that is what I had been promised from the beginning, by the books and the nurses and my own mother on the phone: that the child would be a stranger, and that I would have to learn her, the way you learn a city, by getting lost in it. I had simply been more lost than most.

At home, Paul carried her upstairs and laid her in the crib, and we looked at her together, and she looked at the ceiling, at the shadow of the tree outside our window shifting in the wind.

"She has your mouth," Paul said.

"Does she?" I said, and leaned over to see, and it was true, or it was becoming true. She did.
